text: Every access control rule in ServiceNow, no matter how it was created, is a record on one single table: sys_security_acl. There's no separate permission engine hiding somewhere else in the platform. When a user tries to read an Incident, open a form, run a report, or call a Table API endpoint, the platform looks at that one table for every rule that could apply, and evaluates them before the request goes any further.

Here's the part that trips up almost every new admin: when more than one ACL applies to the same operation, every single one of them has to pass. It's an AND across all applicable ACLs, not an OR. The instinct is usually, if the user matches any ACL that grants access, they're in. That's backwards. If three ACLs apply and two pass but the third fails, access is denied outright, no matter how many others would have allowed it.

This matters constantly in day-to-day administration. Adding a brand new ACL to tighten security on a table never weakens what's already there, but it absolutely can break access that used to work, because now there's one more rule in that AND chain that has to pass too. Admins who don't internalize this spend hours confused about why access used to work, right after they added what they thought was a narrow, unrelated rule.

ACLs are also split by operation. Read, write, create, and delete are each governed by their own separate ACL records, even on the very same table. A user can have full read access to every Incident and still have zero ability to create one, because incident.read and incident.create are entirely different rules. When troubleshooting, the first question is always which operation actually failed.

Table-level checks and field-level checks both run, layered on top of each other. Passing the table-level read ACL gets a user into the record at all, but any field-level ACL on a specific field is checked in addition, never instead. That exact distinction, table-level versus field-level, is where we're headed next.
